name: Wendy Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a team lead at Lantern Fresh, a supermarket that sells a lot of Asian groceries and organic veg, in the busy part of town near the tram stop. I run the self-checkout zone and the click-and-collect packing, so I'm half on the floor, half at the tablet. I start at eight, check the order queue, and I'm usually fixing a scanner jam by half past.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and do you use any AI tools yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love how quick it is. I use AI every day, honestly. It writes my rota drafts, translates our shelf labels into three languages and helps me learn the new stock system. I even use it to plan my own weekends and to practise for a retail-management diploma I'm doing online two evenings a week. My partner Jamie is a freelance graphic designer, which matters a lot to me when I think about AI. We rent together, we've got a strong cushion, about nine months of both our costs, and no kids yet, though we talk about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief and a bit boring, and I'd tell my team the tools we're already using are good enough. At work I'd keep showing people the handy bits, like the label translator. Online I'd probably post a joke about all the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means keep going. My job is scanning, packing orders and fixing the machines, and none of that disappears in a plateau. Jamie's design work would be okay too, though freelance is always lumpy, so I'd still worry a bit about months with no clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my diploma and apply for assistant store manager when it comes up, probably within a year. I'd keep the AI habits going, because they save me hours. And I'd put the savings into an index fund and a small emergency top-up, about three hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, really. Calm. I enjoy the job and I like that I'm learning something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by lumpy freelance work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jamie can earn four thousand one month and eight hundred the next. We run our budget on Jamie's low month, so a quiet spell with no clients isn't a crisis. That's normal for us, and the cushion is basically there for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to coworkers who ignore the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show them one thing that saves them ten minutes, like writing the rota message. I wouldn't lecture. People try things when it's small and it works.

say: I'd tell my team the tools we already use are **good enough**.
I'd post a joke about the **hype** and keep showing people the label translator.
think: My day is scanning, packing and fixing machines, so a **plateau** barely touches it.
Jamie's freelance income is **lumpy**, which is my one standing worry.
do: Finish my retail-management **diploma** and apply for assistant store manager.
Keep my daily **AI** habits, which save me hours.
Put about three hundred a month into an **index fund**.
feel: **Calm**, enjoying the job and the learning.
S0.quote: We run our budget on Jamie's low month, so a quiet spell with no clients isn't a crisis.
fieldNote: Calm rests on a strong **cushion** and a plan, while Jamie's lumpy income is the one pressure she names.
Her advice to **sceptical** colleagues is small and practical, which fits her adaptive style.

steps.text: Finish the online retail-management diploma by next summer
Keep using AI for rotas and label translations
Put three hundred a month into an index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one to get ready for, not to fight. At work I'd run a lunchtime session on how we use the tools. Online I'd share what's working and be honest that some jobs, including a lot of Jamie's friends' jobs, are in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is where it gets personal. Thinking tasks go first, like design briefs, copy and ordering, so Jamie's clients start using AI for the simple jobs and the freelance income drops. My own work is more hands-on, but head office would cut back-office roles and ask us team leads to do more with the tablets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take on the ordering and the stock forecasting at Lantern Fresh so I'm the person who knows the system. I'd move my diploma along faster and ask about a store operations job at head office. And I'd tell Jamie to learn the AI design tools properly and focus on brand clients, not quick logos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy about Jamie and excited about me, and I'd rather say that out loud than pretend I'm only one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Jamie handle it if Jamie's income dropped by half?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cover rent from my pay and the cushion for a while. Jamie would pick up part-time shifts at Lantern Fresh if needed, which they joke about already. We'd cut dining out and the subscriptions, about five hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're enthusiastic about the tools. Where do you draw the line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I draw it at customers' trust. If a tool gives a wrong price or an allergen error, someone could get hurt. I'd always have a person check the labels, and I'd say so loudly.

say: I'd call this the one to get **ready** for, not fight.
I'd run a lunchtime **session** on how we use the tools.
think: Thinking tasks go first, so Jamie's clients start using AI for **simple jobs**.
Head office will cut back-office roles and ask team leads to do **more**.
do: Take on **ordering** and forecasting so I know the system best.
Speed up my diploma and ask about a **head office** operations job.
Cut about five hundred a month from **spending** if Jamie's work dips.
feel: **Uneasy** about Jamie, excited about myself, and honest about both.
S1.quote: I'm uneasy about Jamie and excited about me, and I'd rather say that out loud than pretend I'm only one of them.
fieldNote: Her **optimism** about her own job sits beside a real worry about her partner's exposed freelance work.
She wants humans **checking** allergen labels, which shows where her enthusiasm for the tools stops.

steps.text: Take on ordering and stock forecasting at Lantern Fresh
Apply for a head office store operations role
Cut eating out and subscriptions by five hundred a month
Finish the management diploma a year early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have two years and it isn't enough, and I'd say it plainly at work. I'd tell my team the tools matter even more now, and we should look after each other. Online I'd probably write a long post about what Jamie's world looks like when everything's automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the scary one. Jamie's design work is thinking work, so it could be mostly gone by 2028, and my tills and packing go about three years after. Both of us losing our income within a few years is what keeps me awake. The cushion helps, but nine months isn't enough for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd save as hard as I can, stop all spending we don't need and aim for twelve to fifteen months. Second, I'd try to get a role in store operations or tech support at head office, the people who manage the robots. Third, Jamie and I would talk about moving closer to my parents, where it's cheaper. And I'd lobby my union branch for retraining funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, really. I wouldn't freeze, but my stomach drops when I imagine both of us out of work, but I'd still make a plan, because I always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you consider moving to your parents' town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent there is half and my mum would feed us, to be honest. It would feel like a step back but it's safety. And it's an hour from a bigger city, so there'd still be work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jamie the night this was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not going to panic, we're going to make a list. Then I'd tell Jamie I'd carry the rent for a while and we'd work out the next move together. I'd say it won't be pretty, but we have each other and money.

say: I'd say two years isn't **enough** and say it plainly at work.
I'd tell my team to **look after** each other and keep learning the tools.
think: Jamie's design work could be mostly gone by **2028**, and my tills by 2031.
Both of us losing income is what keeps me **awake**.
do: Save hard and stretch our **cushion** to twelve or fifteen months.
Apply for a **head office** role managing the robots.
Consider **moving** to my parents' town where rent is half.
feel: **Alarmed**, with my stomach dropping, but still making a plan.
S2.quote: my stomach drops when I imagine both of us out of work, but I'd still make a plan, because I always do.
fieldNote: She **expects** both household incomes to be hit within a few years, which puts her at alarmed even with savings.
Her **instinct** to plan and to talk with Jamie is steady, despite the fear.

steps.text: Cut all unneeded spending and save towards fifteen months
Stop subscriptions, holidays and eating out
Apply for a head office role managing store robots
Look at moving to my parents' town where rent is half

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real window and we should treat it like one. At work I'd run a monthly session on skills. Online I'd share training links and be clear about what I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel it first at home through Jamie, around 2031, then my own job around 2034. With five years I think we can adjust, but we'd have to start immediately. I'm anxious because it's two incomes going the same direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use year one to finish the diploma and get into assistant store manager or an operations role. I'd get Jamie training in something that mixes design and hands-on work, like installation or event design. And we'd save about two thousand a month between us and keep the flat rent flexible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's an energetic kind. I'd rather be busy than stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of work would suit Jamie that mixes design and hands-on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shopfitting, signage, exhibition builds, things where you design and then make it with your hands. Jamie's already good with a drill. I think the robots take longer there, since each job is different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change your family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want kids, but I'd wait until we're both on stable ground, maybe thirty or thirty-one. I wouldn't give up the idea, just move it. A kid in a house with two uncertain incomes isn't wise, so I'd move our plans back rather than give them up.

say: I'd say five years is a real **window** and we should use it.
I'd share **training** links and be clear about what I'm doing myself.
think: I'd feel it first at home through **Jamie** around 2031, then at my job.
Two incomes heading the same way makes me **anxious**.
do: Finish the **diploma** and move into assistant manager or operations.
Get Jamie trained in design plus **hands-on** work, such as shopfitting.
Save about two thousand a month between us and keep **rent** flexible.
feel: **Anxious**, but energetic, because I'd rather be busy than stuck.
S3.quote: A kid in a house with two uncertain incomes isn't wise, so I'd move our plans back rather than give them up.
fieldNote: Five years lowers her mood from **alarmed** to anxious, because there is time to rebuild both incomes.
She delays **children** rather than giving them up.

steps.text: Finish the diploma and apply for assistant store manager
Ask Lantern Fresh about a store operations role
Save two thousand a month between us
Put off having children until we're both stable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it. At work I'd use it to help the youngest staff plan. Online I'd write something optimistic but honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough that I'd probably be a store manager by 2033 or doing something else I can't predict. Jamie would reshape their career too. The worry is smaller, but I'd still keep one eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep up my AI habits and finish the diploma this year. I'd aim for store manager by thirty-two, and maybe launch a small side business with Jamie, like a packaging and branding service for local food sellers. We'd also start a family on a normal schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. Ten years is a gift, so I'd use it to try things while I still have savings behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the side business with Jamie look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jamie designs labels and packaging, I know how food gets sold and how shops buy. We'd help small producers get onto shelves. Our first customer could be the cheese maker who sells to Lantern Fresh already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use AI every day for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of course. It would do the first draft of everything, and we'd do the taste. That's the bit I think humans keep for longer, deciding what's good.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** and we shouldn't waste it.
I'd help our youngest staff **plan** their next steps.
think: By 2033 I could be a store **manager** or doing something I can't predict.
The worry is smaller, but I'd keep one **eye** on it.
do: Finish the **diploma** this year and aim for store manager by thirty-two.
Launch a small **packaging** and branding side business with Jamie.
Start a **family** on a normal schedule.
feel: **Calm** and a bit excited to have a decade to try things.
S4.quote: Ten years is a gift, so I'd use it to try things while I still have savings behind me.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **adaptive** curiosity run, and the side business with Jamie turns both their skills into a hedge.
Calm here is earned by time and **savings**, not by denial.

steps.text: Finish the diploma this year and aim for store manager
Start a packaging and branding service with Jamie for local food makers
Keep using AI daily for first drafts
Start a family on the normal timetable

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Two incomes in one household hitting trouble at the same moment, and not enough time to rebuild. What would help is a real warning, retraining you can afford without quitting your job, and employers who don't cut everyone at once.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Customers think self-checkout is just a machine, but somebody has to teach it, fix it and calm the person it just shouted at. I'd say don't treat supermarket staff as the people who get left behind. A lot of us are quick learners and use these tools more than office people think. Give us the same training chances as a graduate, and see what happens.

headlineQuote: Customers think self-checkout is just a machine, but somebody has to teach it, fix it and calm the person it just shouted at.
portrait: **Wendy** is a 27-year-old team lead at Lantern Fresh, a grocery with Asian and organic produce, running self-checkout and click-and-collect.
She is progressive and adaptive, uses **AI** daily and is studying for a retail-management diploma online.
Her partner Jamie is a **freelance designer**, so her worry is two household incomes heading the same way.
She has about nine months saved, and moves from calm in a plateau to **alarmed** if AGI arrives in 2028.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** case, when both she and her partner could lose income at once.
whatWouldHelp: A **real** warning, affordable retraining and employers that don't cut everyone at once.
